theory.overview: A static array is a fixed-size collection of elements stored in contiguous memory locations. Unlike dynamic arrays, static arrays have a predetermined capacity that cannot change after creation. They provide O(1) access to any element via index and are the foundation of most data structures. Static arrays are ideal when the maximum number of elements is known in advance, offering memory efficiency without overhead from resizing operations.

keyConcepts.name: Contiguous Memory
keyConcepts.description: Elements are stored in consecutive memory locations. This enables constant-time access via index calculation: address = base + (index × element_size)

keyConcepts.name: Fixed Capacity
keyConcepts.description: Size is determined at creation and cannot change. Attempting to add beyond capacity causes overflow or requires a new array.

keyConcepts.name: Zero-Based Indexing
keyConcepts.description: First element is at index 0, last at index n-1. This convention simplifies pointer arithmetic.

keyConcepts.name: Cache Locality
keyConcepts.description: Contiguous storage maximizes CPU cache utilization. Sequential access is extremely fast due to cache prefetching.

algorithmSteps.description: Initialize static array with capacity 6, containing 4 elements
Access arr[2] = 30 in O(1) time via index calculation
Insert 25 at index 2: Shift elements right, O(n) operation
Delete element at index 2 (25): Shift elements left, O(n) operation
Linear search for value 30: Check each element until found
Traverse array: Visit each element from index 0 to size-1

minigame.title: Array Operations Challenge
minigame.description: Perform insertions and deletions on a static array. Watch for shifting operations!
instructions: Observe the shifting of existing elements
Delete elements and see how gaps are filled
Understand why static array modifications are O(n)
